en: Flying to Mars takes about seven months.
So why might the very first people who land there never come home?
Take a guess.
I'm Max, and this is Max Wise.
Let's step outside and find out.
Problem one is the air.
It is so thin that the pressure is less than one percent of Earth's.
Without a suit, the spit on your tongue would start to boil, just from your own body heat.
Problem two sounds like fun.
Mars has only thirty eight percent of Earth's gravity, so you could jump almost three times higher.
But over the years, weak gravity slowly weakens bones and muscles.
Problem three is invisible.
Mars has no global magnetic field and very thin air, so far more space radiation reaches the ground.
And if something goes wrong, you can't just call home.
A radio message needs from about three to twenty two minutes to reach Earth, one way.
Now the biggest problem.
No rocket has ever taken off from the surface of Mars.
Not one.
So fuel and oxygen for the trip home must come from Earth, or be made on Mars.
A test machine on the Perseverance rover made oxygen from Martian air.
Over about two years it made one hundred twenty two grams, roughly ten hours of breathing for a small dog.
And even with a full tank, you wait.
Earth and Mars line up for a quick trip only about every twenty six months.
A round trip could take close to three years.
So the first explorers on Mars may stay for a very long time.
Getting there is hard. Getting back is harder.
Stay curious!
